utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Could we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May it please your Honours, my name is Grant Niemann, I appear on behalf of the Prosecution with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan. And may I take this opportunity to request that I may be excused from court for the balance of this cross-examination so that I may speak with our next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may. Can we have the appearances for the defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, attorney from Sarajevo. I am Defence counsel for Zejnil Delalic, together with my co-counsel, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic, I appear on behalf of Zdravko Mucic, together with my colleague, Michael Greaves, attorney from Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Salih Karabdic. I appear on behalf of Hazim Delic, together with my co-counsel, Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas. (Witness enters court) GENERAL JOVAN DIVJAK (continued)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still on oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, you are still on oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My name is John Ackerman, I appear with Cynthia McMurrey on behalf of Esad Landzo. May I inquire who the next witness of the Prosecution is? We are not certain, there are two possibilities at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The next witness is the professor whose last name I would prefer to try not to pronounce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me have some clarification Mr. Delic had his medical examination this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I have been informed that he has. That is what they told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Residovic, can you conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We ended the working day yesterday by my asking you to be shown three documents dated 3rd June, 1992. Since I was informed by the Registry that one of those documents has not been marked, could this document with the same date please be marked, and be shown to the court and the Prosecutor. If it has not been shown to the witness, then to the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked Defence document 130/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Could we have a copy of that document, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We submitted a sufficient number of copies yesterday for the court and the Prosecution. Could a copy be given to the Prosecution, please? These are the three documents that were given to the Prosecution together with the others that we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may just clarify so my Lords are correct. I have two documents, 129 and 130, both are dated June 3rd. I do not have any other June 3rd documents, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, there should be three documents dated 3rd June, two are decisions and one is an order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Documents 128, 129 and 130.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only have the document 130/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Where are the two earlier documents, 128 and 129? (Handed to the witness).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you looked at the documents, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us please look at the document dated 3rd June, 1992, which by name is an order. Do you have that document before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in the upper left corner of this document, does it say that it is issued by the municipality of Konjic, the War Presidency? The number is given and the date of issuance in Konjic, 3rd June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like not to express an opinion about documents which are not military documents. These are not military documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to remind you, General, that I do not expect you to give an expert opinion about this document. I am not asking you to identify this document. I am simply asking you to answer questions which are quite obvious in terms of the format of this document. So if you can, would you please answer my questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I just may object. If it is merely a matter of reading the document, the Prosecution does not see why the witness should have to do it. We certainly have no objection if Ms. Residovic wants to read the document out loud for the court or if the court can read it itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I agree with this objection. If you think it is obvious I do not see why you want him to say anything about an obvious thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After these questions if you feel it is quite sufficient for me to read it or for you to read it, I only have a couple of questions in connection with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If they are questions he can give answers to he would, but not questions for which his opinion he thinks might not be necessary. And in fact it is not in the ordinary course of his business as a General -- it is not in his course of business, so he might not even have to answer any things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has certain expert and personal knowledge, so I will not ask questions which I think that the General cannot answer. But of course he can always say that he does not know. In view of what you have said, General, but the court has allowed me to put the question to you, my question is: judging by what you see in this document, is this document addressed to the co-ordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you please accept my position that I do not wish to comment in any way on a document which does not come under the general framework of combat documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Acknowledging such a position, because the court has allowed you the possibility not to answer such questions, in view of your wish to speak only about things related to military documents, will you please look at the document and tell me whether it has been addressed to the command, and a logistic body of the command. That will be my only question. Is it stated that it is addressed to the command and the logistics command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You said it was obvious, and it is indeed obvious it is to the command, to the logistics body, the Presidency, says one document; the other one, the Red Cross, the civil defence; and the third document says that it has been addressed to the health centre in Konjic, the head of the medical corps, the command, the logistics body, the secretariat of national defence, the Presidency. That is what it says here and I simply read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In connection with these documents that have been marked as Defence exhibits, I have no further questions to the General, thank you. Before you came to Konjic, General, you confirmed that you had no knowledge about any prisons in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I was not familiar with the situation in the territory of the municipalities of Konjic, Jablanica, Prozor, Mostar and particularly -- and therefore I had no information about any prisons, because I had no information at all. I had no personal knowledge about the situation in those areas at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore with reference to your testimony regarding your knowledge about the situation in Konjic, is it correct -- would I be right in saying that you had no personal knowledge as to who and when may have set up prisons in Konjic, including the Celebici prison; who, when and under what conditions stationed guards and other personnel in that prison, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew nothing about these things that you are talking about, about prisons, the way they were secured and any of those other things that you have listed, in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would now like the General to be shown a document which we received from the Prosecution, who again explained that they received it from the Bosnian government. We have sufficient copies for the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. Could the document be marked as Defence exhibit and shown to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence exhibit number D131/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you looked at it, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, is it true that judging by the form and content of this document it is a document issued by the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces in Sarajevo on 27th September, 1992, as indicated in the top left-hand corner of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what is stated in the heading of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this document was signed by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that also at the bottom of this document we see a stamp of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather the Ministry of the Interior of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in the issue of -- in the interest of speeding things up the Prosecution would object to the Defence counsel having this witness read what is on the document. Certainly we have no objection to the court reading it, we in fact have no objection if the Defence counsel wants to get this into evidence. Certainly in closing arguments or written submissions she can point out certain things about the document. But I think it is of no evidentiary value to have this witness read out loud what is on a document that he has not seen before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Actually you yourself have been doing the same, the letter by the Red Cross, he had not seen it before you read it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do not object to her admitting it. I do not object to her asking questions about it. If your Honours think it is helpful to have this witness read it out loud I do not object to that either. I thought it might speed things along rather than have this witness read it out loud. I do not have any objection to her putting questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think that is the request, for him to read it out loud. She can put questions to him based on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to thank my learned colleague for trying to help me to do my job, but I am doing my best to act as I should, and I think I am doing so in accordance with the rules of this Tribunal. Having put the question to the witness, I am not sure whether he confirmed that there was a stamp at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is a stamp that says the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Ministry of Defence, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what is rather interesting and charming and which confirms that we respected multi-ethnicity in the army, there was -- it is in both Cyrillic and Latin script.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, is it true that this document was addressed to the municipal staff of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this document does not say that the same has been submitted to Tactical Group 1, nor is Tactical Group 1 mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that it says to the municipal staff of Konjic. I see nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this document makes no mention of the name of Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not mention the name of Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the witness has answered the questions put by the Defence and since there are no objections to the admission of this document, I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I propose that both the Prosecution and the Defence find the document 01543/1, dated 25th September, to see whose document it is and what it speaks of, because the way in which this document has been given one does not know what was the reason why the Chief of Staff issued such an order. This is not really an order, it is just an approval, agreement with a proposal given by somebody and one does not see by whom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, it is admitted. It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could the General now be shown the next document which the Defence received from the Prosecution, which again obtained it from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have copies for your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document D132/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you looked at the document, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this document also is a document of the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the 25th September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like the previous document addressed to the municipal staff of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, General this document is also signed by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and that it is addressed to the district staff of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that this document makes no mention of Tactical Group 1, nor the name of Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true to say that this document is not an order but an information and a suggestion with respect to the way in which to deal with the particular problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true to say that from this document, as from previous ones, it is clear that already in September certain bodies sought to take steps to create the best possible conditions for the accommodation of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot draw such a conclusion from this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it follows from this document that the person issuing the document believes that the most suitable thing would be to accommodate the prisoners in Zenica, where the prisoners from your territory have been accommodated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like this document also to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is admitted. Actually, I do not know why you ask questions about somebody's opinion about why a thing was done. You are asking him about the writer's opinion of that. He might not be able to give you any account of that. If he wrote it perhaps it might be more sensible to ask such questions. The exhibit has been admitted, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, sometimes we too may be wrong in phrasing our questions. I agree that I should not ask the witness for his opinion, though he has already provided an answer. Thank you, anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just say that in the information which the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command has issued and says that prisoners should be moved from the Celebici barracks in Konjic, so that this barracks may be used for the accommodation of the units in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That is exactly what it says in the document. General, you knew that Zejnil Delalic was a man who had no military training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know now that he is not a man with any military training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He acquired it in the defence of Konjic and the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But General, when you met him you probably learned that he was a man dealing in business, a businessman, and who had -- who was knowledgeable with respect to purchasing goods in the area of logistics and in communication with the business world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met him as a resolute man who is capable of carrying out any task assigned to him by a Superior Command. I did not know, nor in the 37 or 38 days I was with him did I know, that he was a businessman and that he dealt in logistics before, and also, in contact with other people, I learned that he had contributed financially to the defence of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you perhaps know today's Colonel, Pilica Sucro, formerly a Major in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Colonel, formerly a Major, Pilica Sucro, was Chief of Staff of Tactical Group 1, when the Commander was Mustafa Polutak, and at the time you met Zejnil Delalic as Commander of the Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not know that that was the position he held.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you just gave us some of your personal impressions on Zejnil Delalic. During the time you were in Konjic you probably came to know him at least a little bit as a person. General, can you tell me, was Zejnil Delalic as a person a kind of a person who could have agreed to something that would be impermissible, which is what you have said here? But to put it more precisely, did you experience Zejnil Delalic as a person who regardless of the duty that he held, in other words as a person, how would he react if he knew that somebody was engaged in something illegal? You spoke of this in the media and I read about it, so can you confirm this before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not objecting, I am just noting for the record that the Defence counsel is putting the accused's character in issue and the Prosecution will be entitled to introduce evidence in rebuttal concerning that. If she wishes to do that, we do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I hope you understood the nature of the objection, not that you might not put the questions that you want to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You see, if you bring up evidence of good character the opposition can always bring in evidence to the contrary. Normally the reputation of an accused is not relevant, but if an effort is made to bring in evidence of his good character then the other side has a right to say that -- that his character was not good.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the issues of the legal culture is something that is a continuing educational process. I think that my client has nothing to fear by opening such issues, but taking into account the entire proceedings I think that it is not necessary to open this issue now. I know how he feels and I do not wish the witness to actually answer this question at this time. So, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually are you saying that you are withdrawing the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So in conclusion, General, you know, or you may not know, but maybe you can confirm my own knowledge. None of the soldiers under the command of Zejnil Delalic as Commander of the Tactical Group during the combat operations for the lifting of the blockade of Sarajevo did not commit any criminal act and has no connection with the Celebici prison; if I said this, could you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to that question also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose if he has any knowledge about it he could say so. If he has none, he says he knows nothing about that. So he is not in a position to answer either way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about the question as asked by Madam Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. So ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to particularly thank the General. I think he understood that the rules here are very strict, but I know that he and I will have numerous other occasions to talk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only have been learning for three days now, and you said that you have been at it for 19 months, so I will need more time to catch up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed Ms. McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Not translated).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I do not speak French. I think it was nice. I want to thank you for such an esteemed gentleman and an officer from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for being here. I have a few questions that are not really that specific but some things I would like to cover with you. The court knows that you did have an opportunity to visit with all of us back here with the Victim and Witnesses Unit I believe last week one day. We visited briefly at that time, did we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You promised that we would have coffee too, but I am waiting for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That will have to be after you testify. You had mentioned, and I think that you represent something to this court that is very important in the whole understanding of what happened in the former Yugoslavia, and that is the idea that you are a Bosniak. You were a Bosniak, you are a Bosnian citizen, and underneath that, something much less important to you than that, is your religious affiliations, or the religious affiliations of your friends, your neighbours, and the people you live with in Sarajevo, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right, but I only had one problem. Because I was being called Alija Serb, but I was fine with that. Your Honours, Alija is the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they call me Alija Serbs because I stayed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Of course the court knows that you are not the only person of other ethnic background besides Muslim that stayed and fought in the BiH army, right? There were others too, there were Croats and there were Serbs, there were people of other ethnic religions that really are not represented in this argument right now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Besides the Bosniaks and Serbs and Croats there were others. I mentioned that the other day, and I would like to restate there were Jews, Albanians, gypsies -- and when we are done I will tell in private a joke about the gypsies and how they experienced this war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I look forward to having some jokes told, because none of us have laughed enough through this, I know that. I have a few statements that I want you to tell me if in your mind these statements are true, because I believe you will be able to confirm in the mind of a true Bosnian citizen these statements would be true. To call the Bosnian warfare "ethnic" demeans the Bosnian cause by making it seem as if the Bosnians too were just one more narrow ethnic group. That is demeaning to a Bosnian to have this called the "Muslim war", the "Muslim forces", is it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I object as to relevance. I think that this trial should as much as possible stay focused on the issues and not venture into political arenas. So without indicating any disagreement with what Defence counsel is or is not saying, I would ask that we focus on relevant issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might respond, the indictment clearly calls these forces "Muslim forces" and it also refers to the whole situation involved in this which is part of the proof of the Prosecution. So I believe that the opinion of this General about what was stated in the indictment by the Prosecution is very relevant at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It would be -- the opinion would be irrelevant, but can you ask him is that factually what is true. Do not ask him his opinion. He is not an expert on those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, read the portion to him, is that true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You ask the first question, that Bosnia was not really one ethnic group. It consisted of so many different groups and there were so many different groups in the army. You have asked him that question already. Do not ask him his opinion about something somebody else has said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to try to re-phrase it to something I may think be acceptable of what I am really trying to say. What I am trying to say is that to a true Bosniak the fact that this war has been split into ethnic rivalry is offensive, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if you permit a comment -- am I permitted to comment, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Last night I had an opportunity to give a lecture in Leiden on the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and I was very happy to be in such an environment at the university that dates from the 17th century. As I was being introduced by a young man who is a student of political science and diplomacy he said that I would be speaking about the ethnic war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was about the civil war, and I said that had it -- had that been the case I would not have been here now, and as I said the other day I could have been in California or in Alaska. In June 1992 the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted a platform on the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this platform it is clearly spelt out that there was an aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is clearly stated that all patriotic forces should join in the struggle, in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time there was still this forced name. It was from the Austro-Hungarian times where it stated Muslims and Serbs and Croats. The platform spoke about the defence of the multinational, multi-ethnic, multi-cultural Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the armed forces, this platform was implemented and it was the leading light for the young men who were dying for Bosnia-Herzegovina. The other sides, the other two sides, always spoke of it as a Muslim army, that these are the balijas, and yesterday I was asked what language was being used to describe the aggressor on our side, and we issued instructions, and you could see from the document that the Commander sometimes did not use the words that the Presidency enjoined. The Bosnia-Herzegovina would not have survived the aggression of the fourth largest force in Europe had it not based it on multinationality. And I would just like to give you another specific example. As a member of a delegation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I took part in the negotiations with the representatives of the army of the Republika Srpska and also at the beginning of a meeting, whether it was General Mladic, General Gvero or somebody else, some other Commander of the army of Republika Srpska, they made a condition that no traitor of the Serbian people may take part in a Muslim delegation. So it was not a Muslim army, it was Bosnian army, and its main idea was, and it remains to be, the unified Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as it was recognised by the United Nations as its 177th member state. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the people fighting inside Sarajevo, the Territorial Defence inside Sarajevo, one third of those people fighting to protect Sarajevo were Serbs, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a third, but yesterday I tried to give the specific data. In the main headquarters there were 12 per cent Serbs and 18 per cent Croats. There were units -- I remember a battalion who was defending part of Sarajevo which is called the Heros' Square were 25 per cent of Serbs in that unit. Where this unit had been formed there were not that many Serbs living either. I think that in two or three units there may not have been any Serbs, but in most units it was a nice combination. And if you will permit me the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Serbian population, there were people from the Serbian population and from the HVO as well, and I mention two names, Cedo Domuz and Major Petrovic, whom I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am not going to get into all these military details that my colleagues have covered specifically for a long time. A recap on something; if I could have Defence Exhibit 74/1, the map, put back up here for a moment, I would like to ask the General a question dealing with the map, please Mr. Usher. Now, before having you stand up and look at the map again, I just want to go over something that you said in your testimony yesterday -- or maybe it was the day before, I am losing track now -- but number one you referred to the Konjic area of Herzegovina as the pearl -- you referred to the Konjic area of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the pearl of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and that has two meanings to you, I believe. One would be because of its beauty, but number two would be because of its strategic importance in defending the country from foreign invaders. You talked about how Tito's partisans defended the whole country just from this area, is that not true? (Pause). I am sorry, I did not hear any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Besides what you said, that it is both a beautiful place and a strategically important place for me, the most important part is the people there; and I am convinced, and I know, that for decades Croats and Serbs and Bosniaks lived there together. And I know that the experiences from this war -- none of the ethnic groups will ever forget, but they have to forgive. So what I would like to add is the people, and that is an additional quality of Bosnia-Herzegovina, during World War Two the area through the Neretva River valley up towards Sarajevo were battlefields where Yugoslavia was created. I do not know how the world views this, but for us, for us it was a very special battle, when with fierce fighting a hospital with some 3500 wounded was saved in the struggle against the fascist formations of Italy and Germany, and this was precisely in the area of the Jablanica and Konjic, and in this war it again manifested itself that these were strategic areas for the defence of Sarajevo and the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe that two really important battles were in the Konjic area, the one you talked about was the hospital, it is also known as the Battle of the Wounded People, or bitka za ranjenike, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And the second battle, the battle in Sutjeska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in another area but it was also within Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. And of course another ideal of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that came from Tito directly also was the idea of brotherhood and unity. You talked about that all the time as the most important thing that kept the BiH army together, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This touches a raw nerve, if you have lived for a long time by respecting everyone and everybody had a chance. New relationships have been created in the 90s. This idea of brotherhood and unity has faded. But among my generation, the older generation, including the commissioned officers, the principles which had to do with brotherhood and unity were still there at the beginning of the war. However, since the different political party leaders, and now I am giving you my own personal experience, since this principle was in the way of these political leaders, and I am not going to give you any names, but they publicly told their people that the Serbs could no longer live with the Bosniaks, the extremist parts of Croats that the Croatians could no longer live with the Bosniaks, and some who accepted these ideas of the other two sides said now why should we insist that we should all live together, that we should live together with the other two groups. Of course these are the extremists whose ideas still survive, but I am convinced that in the coming years when democracy is re-established in the neighbouring countries -- I am thinking of Serbia Montenegro and Croatia -- the rapprochement will follow as it happened in the war 41 to 45 and in the communal life between 1945 and 1990. I apologise to the Trial Chamber, this is not a political arena, but in order to answer fully I am just simply unable to say a simple yes or no to issues that are so fateful for us in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to have you turn now to the map only for one little clarification and to point out, which I am sure the court is aware of, the strategic importance. Can you point on the map to where Bradina is on M17 between Sarajevo and Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: At Bradina there is a tunnel and it is right next to that Ivan Pass that you talked about that is so important for getting equipment through, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The General did say yesterday if you do not go through this pass you have to cross twelve different passes. That is what the General said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have never seen a man with such a vivid memory. My memory is not as good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He did say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He did say that. You talked about the fact former members of the JNA, who are citizens of Bosnia, who left the JNA and were there, they had this training in guerrilla warfare, it was part of the training, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all formations of the Yugoslav People's Army had in their training programmes partisan warfare, as had members of the Territorial Defence. When every two or three years they would go for training, we would practice procedures from the partisan form of warfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And it is my understanding, and tell me if I am wrong, that you knew a person in the Bradina, a person named Rajko Dordic. Did you know that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not said that so far, but I did know that man.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dordic was an educated, trained man, especially in the art of sabotage, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was one of the best trained in the Territorial Defence in that area, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And he was a known leader of the local Serb resistance in Bradina, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you know he facilitated the arming of the persons in Bradina to fight and secure -- their goal was to secure that area Bradina M17 and cut off transportation between Sarajevo and Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have solemnly declared to tell the truth, so I know nothing about what you have just asked me, but yesterday and the day before I spoke to you about documents which we had seized on the 3rd May, 1992, from the second military district, which show that the Yugoslav People's Army in the barracks around and in Sarajevo, in 1991 and 1992, had armed members of units, the citizens of Sarajevo, of Serb ethnicity. And in the first months of the war in Sarajevo, in many apartments of members of the SDS, arms were found, as well as ammunition and means of sabotage. I repeat I know nothing about the actual engagement and operations of Mr. Dzordic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go on, you did when you were there in October and November 1992, you had made a semi-tour of the area to understand the situation in Konjic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And was part of that tour, did you go to the front-line, and you will have to excuse my pronunciation of the Serbo-Croatian names at Glavaticevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you pronounced it excellently in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. And at the front-line when you were there, what kind of different forces did you see represented there, as far as TO, Croatian, MUP, military police, whatever? Who was present there? Were they all present on that front-line fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were no longer the Territorial Defence because this was October 1992. And I saw police, police belonging to the Ministry of the Interior, which was quite rare, actually. But believe me, I do not remember whether there was a unit of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am going to go on to another subject. I believe that of course the Prosecution had asked you what your former occupation was. I would like for you to tell us now what your current occupation is, as a retired General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am just a pensioner. No, I am joking. It gives me satisfaction to say that I am now working on a project which, thanks to the Tribunal -- though it did not quash the subpoena, I was told today that a UN representative denied that the subpoena had been lifted -- we are helping children who have been orphaned in the war. A foundation was set up already in 1994 and I will have today the opportunity to thank people in the Rotary Club who have provided funds for scholarships for 10 children, for 10 orphans. I should like you to tell you that 32,000 children in the federation are without one parent, and more than 3,000 without both. 1,800 children have been disabled and will suffer the consequences until the end of their days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have one more question, that will be it. Yesterday you stated the single most important factor that contributed to the survival of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army in April, May, June, July and August of 1992 was the patriotism of the citizens and soldiers that defended her. This is the same kind of patriotism that supported the partisans under Tito in 1940 where they were the only European country that expelled the Germans and the Italians and the Croatian Ustasha. What you are saying is the only thing that supported that country at that time, when nobody came in to support it with arms, was an extreme sense of patriotism, is that not correct, and especially the young people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may answer, I think it is nothing -- you are not getting the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand. Could it be repeated, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He did make a statement to that effect yesterday, that it was the patriotism of the people, particularly the young people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He did say that yesterday, I was just re-interposing that important point of this war on the Tribunal. If you believe that he will say, "yes, that is exactly right", then I will pass. Okay. One more time, I want to thank you very much, General, for being here and letting us have this honour of questioning you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, I would like to hear your question, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the end of her cross-examination. I think we were satisfied. That ends the session. Do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it should only take a few minutes but I do have some re-examination

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher. I am showing the General a document dated 18th July. It has been previously provided to Defence counsel. I have extra copies for Defence counsel and the court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor Exhibit 193.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: To re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, on the basis of the arguments of the Prosecution. When I wanted to show the witness certain documents, the objection was that the documents were being shown to the witness for the first time, and that they relate to a period that the witness had said he knew nothing about the events in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him see it and say he knew nothing about the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection, which is this. This appears to be a new document. How can that be said, a new document being introduced at this stage to arise out of cross-examination? It is not a question for re-examination, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let the Prosecution start the re-examination. If this document is relevant to the question, then we will know. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you sir. Sir, does this appear to be a normal document for a head of a Tactical Group, and does it provide any indication of the size of the Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. This question does not follow from any question put during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It definitely does, because much of your question was to show about the nature of a Tactical Group and whether certain persons were involved in the Tactical Group. I do not see how this does not follow. Please, you can put the question. It is a simple straightforward one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We cannot see from this the composition of the Tactical Group, but the Commander who signed it, Zejnil Delalic, appointed persons who would hold duties in Tactical Group 1. It does not indicate the units and the equipment, but it does indicate the command staff, the officers who would be members of Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, does the size of the staff give you any indication whatsoever as to the size of the Tactical Group? I am not asking for an exact number, but can you say anything about whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute, are you talking the staff or the persons? He is actually saying "the following persons". He is not talking about the formations but persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Maybe I worded my question incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: "Performed the duties in the TG1 in Konjic"; "the following persons", not "the following formations of the staff" or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Does the appointment of these persons and their titles give you any indication as to the size or responsibility of the Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The translation again is incomplete. It does not list numbers, it does not say what they have to do to perform the duties. There must be some sentence at the end of this enumeration. Perhaps something is missing. Read it yourself and have a look of it; "to perform the duties of the TG1 in Konjic the following persons". What did they do? There is nothing there at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My copy indicates with respect to each person there is a particular duty assigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have a look at it, I do not think any duty is assigned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You will be asking him things outside the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask as in his military experience if he can say anything about whether or not these persons are given certain tasks by these documents. I will only ask him about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe he has called a meeting of these persons to assist him in the task. It does not say anything at all. It does not say to what person what duty is matched. As I say, maybe the translation is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Since the witness has the relevant military experience I will ask the question to the witness. Can you say whether or not the persons mentioned are given certain appointments pursuant to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For each individual person his duties and obligations are indicated within the framework of the Tactical Group. The first one, Cerovac, he says he is assistant Chief of Staff for operational and training affairs. He should be a person who unites the activities of the staff, or co-ordinates the activities of the staff in making assessments of one's own forces, the terrain, prepare with others proposals for the use of units; and that person participates in the drafting of combat documents. For instance, here it says, "the chief of engineering units".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you had read it very carefully and within the context all it is saying is these persons are to perform the duties in the Tactical Group 1 in Konjic. That is all it is saying, and it is complete. The duties in Tactical Group 1 in Konjic; then you have to go back to the Konjic to tell you exactly what are the duties of the Tactical Group 1. That is all it shows.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, are you able to say anything about the size of the Tactical Group based on the appointments made in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already stated, I do not know the composition, the organisation and the formations coming under the Tactical Group. The number of persons listed here could mean that it is a unit which has jurisdiction in the territory for which the Tactical Group has been assigned, recalling the orders of the 16th July when it was stated that it was responsible for the line Jablanica, Konjic, Tarcin, I think it was, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could have the usher's assistance again and ask the Registrar also for Prosecution Exhibit 127. I have extra copies. I would like one document marked, and 127 shown to the witness. I have extra copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, does it refer to any appointment made in respect of military prisons? That is what I want to find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not see any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a very detailed order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown the documents at the same time. They are very similar, so that my question is the same for both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Could the Defence be given copies too, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor exhibit number 194.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I provided extra copies for Defence counsel. It has been previously provided to them, but there are extra copies. Sir, you were shown several documents yesterday by Ms. Residovic, signed by the head of the TO and the head of the HVO. Sir, is it correct that these documents, which are also, in addition to being signed by those people, signed by Mr. Delalic as co-ordinator, do these documents also indicate that during this time Mr. Delalic had an official position as co-ordinator within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise? Because you are mentioning yesterday's documents, signed by the Commander of the municipal staff, Boric, and the HVO Commander. Are you linking those to these two orders? Could you be more precise, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am not necessarily linking them, sir. Because they are similar -- do these documents indicate that during this period of time Mr. Delalic had an official position signing orders as co-ordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In these two documents it is indicated that the co-ordinator was Zejnil Delalic. However, if I may be allowed to say, in theory at least, I do not know what the practice was, a co-ordinator is not a person that may issue orders. He may only participate in the co-ordination of views between civilian and military authorities. I do not know what the practice was actually, but that is the theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I would like now to have you watch two very, very brief -- one is approximately 30 seconds, one is approximately 1 minute -- excerpts from video. These are from I25 and I46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are they videos we have already viewed?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to -- you have certainly -- I do not know whether or not these particular excerpts have been viewed before. They are directly relevant to re-examination. The videos are in evidence, but whether or not these particular very brief excerpts have been shown ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They ought to be associated with the questions which were questioned and answered and perhaps because of the answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: This is directly relevant to Ms. Residovic's questions where she showed several videos and asked whether this was normal for this time period. She also asked the witness a number of questions about the time period during which the Mr. Delalic was a co-ordinator. The Prosecution had not asked in direct questions about when Mr. Delalic was a co-ordinator since this witness was not in Konjic at this time. Since Ms. Residovic raised that issue at length in cross-examination and showed a number of videos, I would like to show this minute and a half excerpt of video, after which I will have one question for the General concerning those, and that will be the -- then I will have one final question and that will be the end of my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Fresh examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will go for a break and return at 12 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. (11.30 am) (Short break) (12.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us clear this. Mr. Karabdic, I have instructions, information that the doctor has seen your client and he is fit to attend the court for the next session. He is fit to be here, except there are good reasons why he should not be here, and if the doctor so certifies then I see cede to the doctor's views. As long as the doctor thinks he is fit I think there are no reasons why he should not be here. I think I should mention that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your information, your Honours. But my client was unwell, and he thought that the same symptoms were reappearing and that is why he asked to be examined by a doctor. Certainly he wants to attend the hearings, and this medical check-up should have no affect on the proceedings or on his presence at the hearings. So that I will take care that he should come, if not today then tomorrow morning for sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What I am saying is he has to be here during the trial, except if there are medical reasons certified by the doctor that he should not be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Certainly. I apologise, your Honours. He asked for this examination, thinking that he would need treatment and not in order to be excused from the hearings. That was his intention; and of course I fully accept what you have told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to express my concern that we are not creating what I would see as a dangerous precedent. I think the Rules are very clear, that a defendant should be here at least during any part of the trial that might affect his interests. We have on occasion asked Mr. Landzo to be excused when the evidence had absolutely nothing to do with his case. But when the evidence has something to do with Mr. Landzo's case, if he is ill, it would be my position that the trial should not go forward without his presence. I hope we are not creating by the Hazim Delic matter some kind of exception to the rules that would be applied against the rest of us. I think it is not fair for a trial to proceed in the absence of a defendant when matters are going on in the trial which affect his trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have orders for this comment. I have made it clear any accused persons in this Trial Chamber who would be affected by the proceedings ought to be here, except if there are medical reasons for him not being here, and in that case the counsel should be here. The whole party should not be absent from the proceedings. Mr. Niemann, have you anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I wish to announce the appearance of Mr. Dixon at the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Nice to meet you. Can we have the witness now? (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, your Honour. If I just may have the two very brief excerpts shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, your Honours, I have an objection. Ms. McHenry said that she was showing these videos because the Defence, in the course of the cross-examination, showed the witness video films from the period when my client was a co-ordinator. I showed the witness films only from the period when he was Commander of Tactical Group 1, that is August, September and October. Therefore there are no grounds in view of the cross-examination to show these videos. Therefore, I showed only videos from August, September and October, the period when Mr. Zejnil Delalic was Commander of Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, are you not sure that the video that she is now trying to show arises from your own cross-examination? Because if it does, then she can still show it, and then correct whatever gaps are still outstanding from your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, that is just what I am saying, because Ms. McHenry, the learned representative of the Prosecution, explained that they did not want to show videos from the time that my client was a co-ordinator. But since I did that, they are using that -- those grounds to show these videos. But I insist that I only showed videos from the period when my client was Commander of Tactical Group 1, August, September and October. Therefore, there are no grounds for the Prosecution to show any videos from another period. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If it would help clarify, I am happy to respond. Maybe I did not -- if your Honours would like me to respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me hear you, because I think you are only entitled to re-examine on issues which arise from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, I am in entire agreement with you. Either I was not sufficiently clear or there was somehow an interpretation issue. I had certainly -- I am not saying that Ms. Residovic showed videos from the time period during which he was a co-ordinator. I certainly I am saying, though, that she asked a number of questions and showed the witness a number of documents regarding the period during which he was co-ordinator. So if there is relevant evidence concerning that period of time in the videos, I am certainly entitled to show it, whether or not it is a document or a video. There is no rule that says nor -- I think it would be against common sense to say because she did not show a particular videotape about that area I cannot. She certainly raised the issue and showed documents about that. I believe these videos, which are less than a minute and a half, are directly relevant to the period during which the accused was co-ordinator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I agree with you, the question is whether there is an issue which has arisen from the cross-examination. If it does then you are entitled to correct it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not think there is any dispute that an issue arose during cross-examination about the period during which he was a co-ordinator. I would ask the video people to show just the two brief excerpts, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not ask a single question with reference to the period, but I referred to a specific document. If this is linked to my questions, then of course I have no objection. But I will object if this video does not refer to my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it does not refer to your cross-examination or relate to it in any manner it is completely out of the issue, it should not be admissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If we may please have the video now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Translating videotape) "Our guest tonight is Mr. Zejnil Delalic, Commander of the Konjic Territorial Defence. Good evening. "Good evening. "What brings you to Zagreb? "There are many reasons. First of all, because the club of the Konjic people which has been formed in the last few days following the aggression against the town of Konjic and its surroundings, and I am also here to sort out some assignments for the Republican TO headquarters regarding the communication system, since as is well known the lines were brutally cut in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the last week or so."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence did not ask a single question relating to this. (Video played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Translating videotape). "Everything is ready. Padalovic reporting, sir. Soldiers, Selam Alakom, Alakom Selam. At ease. Do you know who is imprisoned in Sarajevo? Babo? What do you have to do to liberate Babo? Where will you take him? To Konjic. That is it. Are you the same soldiers who have liberated the area from our enemy. We are. Captain, take over the command. Yes, sir."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, in these excerpts you have seen is Mr. Delalic acting --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object, because none of these subjects does not follow from the cross-examination of the Defence. There were no questions from this period, nor from these -- about these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There are no questions indicating that he is Commander of the territorial group? If that is your suggestion, then no questions indicating, or any documents indicating, that he has any relationship with the territorial group 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with Tactical Group 1 there were many questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose that is what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not a single question. This is the period when he was co-ordinator. I did not ask a single question whether Zejnil Delalic was Commander or co-ordinator in that period. I did not ask any question to that effect to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic certainly asked questions about Mr. Delalic's command responsibility, or lack thereof, during the period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Seriously speaking, is this an issue now which has been doubted? Is anybody challenging that he is Commander of the Tactical Group 1? Is anybody denying that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. I believe that is not in dispute. These videos I think were taken during the period that Mr. Delalic was co-ordinator, before he became Commander of the Tactical Group. As is stated in the indictment, Mr. Delalic was first co-ordinator and then Commander of Tactical Group 1. He is charged with having command responsibility for both periods. Ms. Residovic in her cross-examination introduced documents from that period, before he was Commander of Tactical Group 1, and suggested that the documents, both with the documents and her questions, suggested that those documents establish that Mr. Delalic never had official or de facto authority. I believe these videos are directly relevant to Mr. Delalic's de facto authority. This witness, as a military man, can give his opinion as to what he saw in these videos. If Ms. Residovic wants to agree that Mr. Delalic had de facto command authority during the time period he was co-ordinator then the issue is not in dispute then I would withdraw the questions. Ms. Residovic can correct me if I am wrong, I believe that is an issue that she does dispute.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the response of the Prosecution may be made if I introduced questions regarding Zejnil Delalic as a co-ordinator or Commander of the Territorial Defence in the cross-examination or if the answer that the witness gave me was imprecise. But I think that the witness gave me very precise answers, and I see no grounds for asking additional questions in the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not think you need bother. I think I sustain the objection. It is not necessary, the issues here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I have one question, please, my objection is noted.. Sir, is it the case that even as late as the end of November 1992 the Red Cross was trying to have Celebici closed down as a prison camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can repeat what I saw, and I do not know whether the Red Cross requested that it be closed down. I said that at the end of October and the beginning of November when members of the International Red Cross were being seen off Mr. Zejnil Delalic said that they had toured the facility and that he had no suggestions or instructions as to any special measures that need to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I understand your answer. My question is: at the end of November did you receive any other information about what the Red Cross and what it wished, what it was trying to do regarding Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think my answer was that on the basis of orders transmitted by the Chief of Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina the military prison in Celebici was to be disbanded, and that I participated in drafting that order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And sir, during that time did you receive any information about any request by the Red Cross that the prison be closed down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Be more specific. Information from what source?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, were you specifically told by people, including from the Supreme Command, that the Red Cross wanted Celebici closed down as a prison camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that we had received orders that measures be taken for the camp to be closed down. In the meantime, I have been offered documents here from which I now see that at the request of the municipal staff of the armed forces of Konjic, that at the request of the Chief of Staff of the armed forces, there were suggestions for this prison, or rather the detainees, to be transferred to the prison in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I am not asking you about your documents now. I am asking you, at the end of November did you receive any information that the Red Cross had asked the Bosnian authorities to close the camp down? Did you receive any information regarding that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: General, let me find out one simple fact from you. I am sure you might know. Under whose authority was the Celebici camp at the time you went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, but in view of the communications I had with the municipal headquarters, and in view of the fact that it is regulated by our legislation that military prisons should be formed at that time, at the level of the municipal headquarters of the armed forces, it should have been under the command of the municipal staff of the armed forces of Konjic. And how it actually was at that time, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am still not too sure about who has responsibility for what is happening in that camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who were in the camp are responsible for what was happening in the camp and those who were superior to them. And in view of all that I have insight into, it should have been the Commander of the municipal headquarters of the armed forces in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. Who is the Commander who was -- at least at the time you went there, who was the Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time the Commander of the municipal headquarters of the armed forces of Konjic was Mirsad Catic, as far as I can recall. I know that I co-ordinated with him most when dealing with the municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And is he directly responsible to the supreme chief of the army, Halilovic, or he is responsible to someone else before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time he was the most senior in that area. In these past three days in our discussions we have not established whether the municipal staffs of the armed forces were within the Tactical Group 1. If they were a part of Tactical Group 1, if these municipal staffs were a part of the Tactical Group, then the Commander of the municipal headquarters is responsible for combat readiness, for the situation in the armed forces to the Commander of Tactical Group 1. I do not know whether the municipal headquarters was under the command of Tactical Group 1, nor whether the same can be said of the municipal headquarters of Prozor, Jablanica and Hadzici, which were also in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is all we have for this witness. I do not know how to thank you sincerely on behalf of everyone here. We have been grateful you have patiently taken all the questions in humour and we appreciate your assistance. I think you are discharged now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I say just one sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should like to thank you for the attitude taken towards me by your Honours as a witness; but I should like to take advantage of the opportunity when I return to Bosnia-Herzegovina to convey a very important conclusion. Even though we in Bosnia-Herzegovina may believe that with respect to the war crimes, committed mostly against Bosniaks, and that the work to deal with it is rather slow and that all the culprits will not be tried, I know the motto of lawyers that justice is slow but it comes eventually. I know that all the war crimes committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia will be punished and that will be supported and welcomed by all those who hold peace dear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I call Constantine Economides.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: (Not translated).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we are waiting, right after we returned from the last break we were handed a document of 54 pages that is an English translation of a document that was provided to us two or three days ago in French. In addition we were handed an eight page CV for Professor Economides. Before that all the Prosecution have provided us with was that very short, two paragraph description of Mr. Economides that I showed the court the other day. I think it is in violation of all of the obligations of the Prosecutor under the Rules of this court, and under the interpretation of those Rules by the Court in the Blaskic case, to be providing us with this material in effect five minutes before the witness is to take the stand. This makes it absolutely impossible, and if not impossible certainly unlikely that Defence counsel have any opportunity to prepare for a comprehensive and efficient cross-examination of this witness. I have no idea, and I will not suggest that this was done intentionally by the Office of the Prosecutor so as to prevent us having information. I do know this: that the Prosecutor's office notified this court, I think well over a month ago, of their intention to call this man. It is very difficult for me to accept that this material could not have been provided to us until five minutes before he is to take the stand. I think there are a number of remedies available to the court. One of those is to totally refuse to permit him to testify, because of the Prosecutor's violation of their obligations under the rules. A second is to adjourn the court for a reasonable period of time to permit us to assimilate and explore the new information provided to us this morning. There is a wealth of information about this witness contained on these eight pages that we received literally after the last break, as we came back in from the last break. I think it extremely unfair for this matter to go forward at this point without us having the opportunity even to read, let alone explore, the additional information that was provided to us literally five minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the information, the large document referred to was provided to the Defence in an official language of the Tribunal. The English translation of it was provided to -- we received it today, and the same with the CV. A CV was provided in the language of the Tribunal, and an English version of the CV was also just provided to us this morning. The bundle of documents that I have in front of me was provided to the Defence as soon as we were able to put them together, which was on Friday, I understand, your Honour. So to suggest that we gave a one page document and that is all that we gave was incorrect. Further, your Honours, the Defence have had the telephone number of Professor Economides and Professor Economides is certainly an expert witness and I would be extremely surprised if he had refused to provide the Defence with any information they would have sought from him. In my submissions, your Honours, the Defence have had the information. Certainly, the decision to call this witness and the decision to call this witness was made belatedly by us and so the information was not available to us, and certainly not available to us in one piece; but as we received it we provided it in a timely fashion, and in my submission, your Honours, the Prosecution has done all that it can do in order to provide this information. As I say, and I confirm, the large document, the Venice Commission document, was provided in a language of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, one slight possible correction. I believe Mr. Niemann said that this notebook was provided to us on Friday. In fact, Friday was a holiday; although I was around the Tribunal I sure did not see him or anyone from the Prosecutor's Office here. Secondly, our records show we received it on the 27th (which is a day I am very familiar with because it is my daughter's 18th birthday), that was Monday. The court has been in session pretty much continually since Monday. We have had sessions Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and although I took part of yesterday afternoon off to go through this, this is a fairly massive document, just one document in specific is a document from the International Law Commission, and it appears to have 160 pages. That is one of several documents in here. That is a lot of material to try to go through to disseminate, to just digest it, just read it, let alone -- you get heartburn trying to digest that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must say that before I said that I was unwilling to -- let me just say it this way: Mr. Niemann has now I think deliberately sought to mislead this court. He has told you that this CV that I complained about was provided to us several days ago in the French language, which is one of the languages of the Tribunal. Let me show you. This is a two-page document which is the French CV, that is what was provided to us. (Indicates). So to the extent you were being told by Mr. Niemann all the new one is is a translation of this document, that is extremely misleading. We got a two-page French CV two or three days ago. This one is eight pages long in English. It has a wealth of information that is not contained in that French one. The second thing, lest you think that the delay in giving us this document had something to do with needs of translation in the Office of the Prosecutor, this document comes from the European Commission for Democracy Through Law and was originally published in English and French.
