The other thing you need to know is the Registry has not provided our offices with a French translator and we have a very difficult time getting documents translated from French because we do not have anyone to do that for us. Whether or not we should have known about certain things is really kind of beside the point. We did not. If we had translated this two-page document so that we all could have read it, this two-page French CV, it still would not have given us this eight page document that they gave us just a few minutes ago. I am now beginning to think it may be deliberate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to add something else, we were told this document given in English in Strasbourg is the same as the document given to us in this notebook; this is somewhat incorrect. This is that is a 30-page document, this is a 95 page; the one we were just given is a 95-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Moran, do you not think we should find a way to ameliorate the situation instead of grumbling about what has happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I concur completely with your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In that case, I will sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought so, because we have discussed it for the past 10 minutes and that is not what we think might help. I think there might be a violation of the procedure for doing these things but that is a spilt milk now, we cannot talk about it. There are ways of saving it. Possibly we hear the witness and then postpone his cross-examination to a time perhaps you might be able to digest whatever preparation you may have made. I know you cannot gobble down all these things as you want to. I think that might be a way to save the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at least for -- on behalf of Mr. Landzo I am in fundamental agreement with your Honour. I agree with what you just said. Let me just, so that we do not have this same spilt milk problem as we go down the road in this case, advise your Honours that the Prosecution has not provided us, and we have made more than one request and finally have made a request through the Office of the Registrar, for all of those published writings of Dr. Gow that are contained in the CV that the Prosecution presented to us. We believe under the language of the Rules and the ruling in the Blaskic case that previous writings of witnesses relevant to their testimony are to be turned over by the Prosecutor, in accordance with the Rules. Our plea to the Office of the Registrar was that from an economic standpoint it would cost this Tribunal a great deal less for the Prosecutor to make copies of those writings and turn them over to us than for us to go through the more and sometimes prohibitively expensive job of trying to gather them all up ourselves from sources all over the world. It may be the Prosecutor will represent to you they do not have them, then that is not any longer a matter of concern, although I suspect that they do. I just want to forestall this same kind of problem coming up perhaps Monday, when Dr. Gow arrives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now can we have your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Professor Economides. I would just like to indicate that the material was provided on the 27th. We received it on the Friday. It was copied then provided on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Possibly, therefore, the effort to get them was not made much earlier than that or was not actively pursued. If you knew there was an obligation to serve the Defence with it at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As I understand, the obligation does not arise until we receive it; if we did not have it in the possession we did not have any obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When you made the obligations, you make quite serious efforts to get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We did not have it, your Honour. (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear the witness. PROFESSOR Constantine ECONOMIDES, (sworn).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may take your seat now. Examination-in-chief by Mr. Niemann

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Constantine Economides. I am a Greek national. I am a Professor of international law in Athens at the University of Pantion in Athens. I have spent my career completely in legal service for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, for which I was the head for about 17 years. I am a member of the Venice Commission, which is an organ which is subsidiary of the Council of Europe and which deals with issues dealing with development of democratic institutions. The exact commission is the European Commission for Democracy Through Law.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you a graduate of the Faculty of Law and Political Sciences of the University of Strasbourg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you hold the Diploma of the Centre for Higher European Studies of Strasbourg, which you received in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Nods).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you hold a Doctor of Laws of the Faculty of Law of the University of Strasbourg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And of the Athens University?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you a lecturer of Public International Law at the Faculty of Law of the Athens University?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you an Associate Professor of International Law at the Pantion University of Social and Political Sciences -- I am sorry, were you an Associate Professor, then becoming a Professor in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, yes. Now I am a full Professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And have you been a Member of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman and degrading treatment or punishment since 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I still am.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you a Member since 1990 and were you formerly Vice President of the Venice Commission for Democracy through Law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And are you a Member of the International Law Commission since 1st January this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am a Member of the International Law Commission since the date you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your career, have you participated in bilateral negotiations on behalf of the Greek government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many bilateral negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: With respect to Czechoslovakia in 1964?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Romania in 1966, Yugoslavia in 1974 to 1975?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: USA in 1975 to 1976?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Turkey in 1976 to 1979?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And Italy in 1988?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Bulgaria in 1973?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And again in Yugoslavia in 1973, in relation to a Consular Agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you head of the Greek delegation in negotiations with Poland in 1976, Hungary in 1977 and the Soviet Union in 1978?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Czechoslovakia in 1980?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The German Democratic Republic in 1982?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And Tunisia in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And were you head of delegations in negotiations with Egypt in 1986?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Hungary in 1987, and Morocco in 1988?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you head of the Greek delegation in negotiations with Germany in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Croatia in 1993, Slovenia in 1994, the Czech Republic in 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Russian Federation in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Slovakia in 1995, on the Convention of Status between Greece and the above mentioned countries, as a result of state succession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm everything that you have just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Have you participated in international conferences and meetings; in particular, were you a Member since 1962 of the various Committees of Experts of the Council of Europe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The 20th Extraordinary Session in Rome 1973, of the ICAO on International Aviation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you Chairman of the Committee of Experts of the Council of Europe for the Examination of the Draft of the International Law Commission on the Most-Favoured Nation Clause in 1979?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Nods). Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Representative of Greece to the Special Committee of the Charter of the United Nations and the Strengthening of the Role of the Organisation, 1979 to 1981?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: A member of the Greek delegation at the Third Conference of the United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea, 1980?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: A representative of Greece in the United Nations conferences on succession of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, Defence was referring to some views expressed in Blaskic case. I am not aware of what those views were. The Defence had referred to that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what we were referring to is this that clearly, in our opinion, an article that I publish or that Mr. Niemann publishes on a subject that is relevant to something I am going to testify to is my statement and that our position would be if that article is in the possession of the Prosecutor, the Office of the Prosecutor, it should be given to us. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE

But what I am saying I do not think there is an obligation on the Prosecution to provide you with the articles or books written by an expert. utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As to Professor Economides, I am not really sure, from looking at his resume. I am not even sure what he is going to say today, to tell you the truth. If the Prosecutor is in possession of nose prior writings, it sure would save everybody a lot of time, trouble and effort if they made copies of them, rather than us having to pay hundreds of dollars to run them down and get them off computers and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: An academic writer can take opposite views of topic. In this article he might take one view in another article, a direct opposite view, depending on his view and the materials at his disposition at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Of course, your Honour, if witness X were to take -- were to say A in an article and B on the witness stand then at that point that article would come exculpatory material they would have to produce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not necessary, because it is not a decision and it is not based on any particular facts on which you rely. An article is an article sometimes even thought up by the academic writer himself from what he thinks it ought to be, not necessarily from any particular facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is true, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So what does it have to worry so much about it. When a matter comes before the court with particular facts that is what is relevant. The opinion of an academic writer might be relevant; I say might be, because it can easily be ignored.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I agree as to a third party writer. It is when they appear as an expert and their opinion here differs from their opinion some place else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the witness now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to respond to Judge Jan's question about Blaskic. We do not have them, and the Prosecution has not given us, and it may take some time to get our hands on it. I think Mr. Greaves may have more to say about that particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May I just correct something for the record? The issue in the Blaskic case which primarily occupied Judge Jorda is that the Prosecution had given the wrong spelling of the name of the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, could you explain to the Chamber the nature of the work which you conducted when you were a member of the Venice Commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Apparently the earphones are not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it working, are you hearing anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Then will you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Venice Commission, as I said this morning, was an organ of the Council of Europe. It was established from eastern and central Europe to assist those countries to move forward towards democracy. Its essential purpose was to study the constitutions and draft constitutions, to study constitutional courts, the major internal law drafts. But issues also of international law, which would be of more general interest for that specific country. As part of the study of the international issues the Venice Commission indicated what relation there was between international law and internal law, as was pointed out this morning, and the Venice Commission also reviewed the issue of those cases of state succession and the repercussion of state succession on physical persons. I had the honour of being one of the reporters of the Venice Commission, doing its work. The Venice Commission, in order to come up with a text which represented its declaration, set up a complete questionnaire which was distributed to all the members and to those members -- all the States that were the members of the Council of Europe. The States answered the questions and on the basis of the answers we drafted a draft statement, which I have with me. This work was done with a great deal of care after an investigation which was very detailed, on the part of all the states which answered the questionnaire and on the basis of those questions, that is the practice of the states, allowed us to set up a draft declaration, having to do with state succession and the nationality of physical persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Professor, can I just, before I go to my next question, may I ask you to speak as slowly as possible because the -- what you say must be translated into a number of languages, and there are -- it is a very difficult process if you speak very quickly. Can I ask you if you could speak slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What was the nature of your work then with the International Law Commission, Professor, what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The International Law Commission began that year to review the same questions, except that its purpose -- the title was a little different. The title of the International Law Commission was Nationality of Physical Persons as Relates to State Succession. But in fact the issue was the same. This year the International Law Commission was able to adopt at the first reading a draft article on the issue. The Commission's work was done as follows: the reporter of -- the special reporter, that is -- he would present a very, very detailed volume and a draft article and then the other members of the Commission reviewed it, article by article, that is the entire draft, and at the end would reach adoption of draft order -- a draft which was accepted the first reading. It was not a definitive draft, it was still a draft which still has a great deal of work it requires before it can be adopted definitively. It must first be reviewed by the Legal Commission of the United Nations, which is being done right now, during the General Assembly session. Afterwards, next year, the various states will make their comments on the draft articles. Then, based on the observations of the 6th UN Committee and the observations of other states, the International Law Commission will review once again the same question so that it may be adopted during the second reading. This will be done in about two or three years, perhaps even longer. Once this draft has been adopted in the second reading it will be sent to the United Nations General Assembly which will convene an international conference to adopt a convention on the question. Therefore, this procedure has been launched and the fact that a draft at the first meeting was already adopted, a draft which has a certain weight, and the International Court of Justice even has cited the work of the International Law Commission, which is at a prior stage than the one reached during the first reading. As far as I am concerned, I was involved in this review, and I must say that I was an active participant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Professor, did there emerge, from your work in both the Venice Commission and the International Law Commission, a general consensus of what was understood by the word or term "nationality"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that as regards the concept of nationality there would no -- there were no differences of opinion. There was a total agreement, a general consensus. Nationality, according to all definitions which carry weight, is a legal condition which links an individual to a state, that is the link of nationality. Of course, nationality as a matter, as a question falls under the jurisdiction of states, state jurisdiction. Several years ago it was thought that it was an exclusively national issue. Now the issue has been looked at again and the question of nationality is part of state, but under the limits that have been set by international law. A specific case which illustrates this. Therefore there are states, or states are the ones who are those who have jurisdiction over nationality, and they are the ones who can say, through their laws, who their nationals are, who their citizens are, each state. This was a sovereign right of each state, that it designates who its nationals are. But the designation must be done according to international law, and there we find very well known criteria. There is the question of territory, there is the question of soil, there are the criteria of jus soli, jus sanguis. The child of somebody can have his father's nationality and therefore can be Greek or Italian, if his father is Greek or Italian. It is even the naturalisation process that there are certain people who are not nationals but foreigners, but are connected to a specific territory and can, under those conditions, obtain the nationality of the state through the naturalisation process. This is a process which is very well known and I do not think there were any discrepancies in this concept as far as nationality goes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did the International Law Commission or the Venice Commission of which you were part determine what obligations in particular applied to states when it comes to the issue of nationality and nationality laws?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that there were three essential obligations which existed in international practice and have existed almost for ever, at least since the last century, and these obligations were indicated by the Venice Convention and by the International Law Commission; perhaps not always in the same terms, but there were three obligations which are very fundamental and they are: each individual who is involved in a state succession has the right to have a nationality. It has been considered that the rights to nationality are rights of the person, of human rights proclaimed by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and recently as well by the Council of Europe. As far as nationality is concerned, this was specifically proclaimed and nobody would challenge the legal basis of that, as this person would have the right to nationality. And the principles specifically apply in state succession. These great principles, when there is state succession, are cases in which states as far as possible must try to avoid statelessness. Statelessness would be considered as an undesirable condition which in some way is rejected, so that people do not become stateless after a state succession. That is the first principle. And the second one is very intricately connected, because one would have normal nationality, no longer be statelessness, but these two principles exist in the law of state succession. The third principle is that the state which grants its nationality to a person or group of persons must respect the will of those persons. Respect for will is also an essential rule which has been gaining more and more ground in international law, and this is the third rule, I could say, of the right of the law of state succession, which has been codified, if I could express myself that way, by the Venice Commission and by the International Law Commission in their work. And the clarification of the International Law Commission, that the purpose of the International Law Commission was the codification and the progressive development of international law. So these are the three obligations which are absolutely fundamental to state succession.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Has the issue of nationality gained prominence in recent times in the international community, and if so, why has that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The issue of nationality always is a very basic one, for the international community and for international law as well, and primarily so for international law, in as much as international law is based on states, it is state -- the law between states. The state rests on its population and the population is mainly consisting of nationals for each state. Therefore, the nationality designated nationals of one state is, as it were, at the basis of internal law, but also of international law. It is therefore of very high relevance. Nationality also is important in international law, with regard to humanitarian law. For instance, the nationality of a person will determine the rights that can be applied. Recently, with the emergence of conflicts across ethnical groups, ethnic groups, various groups, there are increasing problems in determining the nationality of a group of people, persons belonging to this or that group, and this gives even more importance to this question, makes it even more difficult to deal with. But these are recent events, relating to recent historical developments. Nevertheless, in this respect we often come across very tough problems when it comes to nationality. International law is more and more at loggerheads and is trying to find solutions to the problems. The present codification might help and assist in sorting the problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Professor, during the course of your involvement with the International Law Commission and the Venice Commission, did you look at the issue of state succession in the context of the former Yugoslavia as one of the examples that you considered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The case of the former Yugoslavia was mentioned, for instance by the special reporter, who mentioned it several times. But the members of the commission, myself included, did not look into it particularly. It was quoted, cited as an example but it was not surveyed by the members of the commission, but special reporter took account of that example, of that case, when it stated the examples, because it really listed all the recent examples, including those concerned by the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Professor, during the course of a state succession what nationality do the residents of the territory of the successor state who were nationals of the predecessor state assume?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, I am going to object to this. I believe they are collaterally estopped from getting into this issue because the appellate decision in the Tadic decision -- I believe it is paragraph 77, but do not hold me to that number specifically -- held that Bosnian Serbs are citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the meaning of your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are trying to relitigate an issue which has already been authoritatively decided by the appellate Chamber. It is essentially a collateral estoppel issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not necessarily the issue. All the expert is giving is his knowledge of the subject matter from every authority and the Lord above. If this is one of the authorities he is using that is a different matter. He is not bound to ignore an authority because it is still in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I do not think that in this court that is in dispute. I think the Appeal Chamber has ruled it is binding on all of us here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He is not giving evidence of matters which are in dispute. He is giving evidence of matters on which his expert knowledge is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: My objection is overruled, your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, do you need me to repeat the questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, remind him of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My question is, during the course of a state succession, what nationality do the residents of the territory of a successor state who were nationals of the predecessor state assume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can give you a very categorical answer, and I am talking about a rule, a legal standard, which, according to the prevailing opinion, has the value of rule of international customary law and this is the rule. The successor state must grant its nationality to all nationals of the predecessor state habitually residing in the territory of the successor state. Therefore, there is an obligation to grant the nationality without any discrimination whatsoever to all nationals of the predecessor state, those nationals being attached, linked to the territory, having their permanent habitual residence in the territory of the successor state. That is the more stable, the most solid rule in state succession.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How significant is the issue of avoiding statelessness in this consideration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Statelessness is a second element in succession law. The Venice Commission and the ILC have established rules that enable us to face the problem and to cope with the problem of statelessness. There is that one rule that I have just spelled out, that the successor state is entitled to grant nationality to anybody residing in its territory. That is a rule that is against statelessness, a rule that is such as to rule out the problem of statelessness. But there are other cases and rules for statelessness. The most important rule is that, in spite of the fact that the state granted its nationality to all residents in its territory, should there be other people who become stateless due to the succession of states, the successor state has to grant the nationality, its nationality, to those people who became stateless because of the state succession. These are very specific cases, but the rule is as I stated, and it is to be found in the declaration of the Venice Commission and more generally to be found in the draft articles of the ILC. Therefore, the state must simultaneously grant its nationality to everybody but also fight statelessness, but grants its nationality to those who become stateless because of the state succession.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In addition to that, is there a right of option to nationality in the context of state succession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. According to traditional practice the right of option has been established for a long time. It was anchored in international treaties concluded after state succession, or running parallel to the succession of states. But this right of option is becoming increasingly more important due to the development of the various theories regarding human rights. The European Convention on Nationality, which I have quoted already, stated expressly in Article 18 that the successor state must grant its nationality, and criteria have to be fulfilled, including that of the will of the person. In other words, each state must endeavour not to grant its nationality against the will of the people concerned. Now, when it comes to the right of option, there used to be a mechanism which probably remains the prevailing mechanism -- this is my personal view, others might not be of this view -- by which the state which is the successor state is entitled to grant its nationality to everybody, regardless of the question of the will of the person. But should the state after a certain time realise that there are indeed groups of people who do not want of that nationality for one reason or another, then the state must, within a reasonable period of time, grant a right of option for those people to express themselves for keeping the nationality of the successor state or for the acquisition of the nationality of the predecessor state, for instance, or of a new state should the predecessor state cease to exist. So, according to this scenario, the right of option applies, but it applies only after a certain period of time has elapsed. The International Law Commission on this issue wants to be a bit stricter. It wants that right of option, and the work is not completed yet, but the ILC wants the right of option to be more immediate; if possible, it wants it to be applicable as of the succession of states, within or without undue delay. This is a trend that comes on top of a very constant and solid practice which I have just sketched out. So after a reasonable period of time there can be this right of option, but the trend is for that right of option to be exercised as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Professor, how important is the will of persons concerned in deciding whether to grant a right of option?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The will of persons is a criterion that is gradually gaining ground. It is quoted by the Council of Europe as one of the decisive criteria when it comes to granting nationality. This criterion sort of is issued from the human rights, is under the human rights. There are two principles. You may not deprive somebody arbitrarily of his or her nationality. This has been anchored in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The second principle is that you can not grant somebody a nationality against that person's will. It can be done, but only for a short or relatively short period of time until matters are settled by the right of option, as I have just said. In the last century the right of option was already an important concept, but remained secondary. But it is gradually and presently becoming a very relevant issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Professor, are you able to give us some examples of where this right of option has been granted, instances where it has occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the peace treaties signed after the First World War, be it the Treaty of Versailles, Trianon, The Hague Convention; all treaties signed after the First World War had the right of option for population that followed the territory that was attached to another state whilst those populations belonged ethnically to another state. So such rights were granted quite broadly to all such populations in Germany, Poland, in many instances to grant the right of option within reasonable period of time. It was a very common practice, well established practice after the First World War. Such practice was also adopted by my country. Greece had five successions of states. There was first the creation of the Greek state, and then there were territories added to Greece, transfer of territories on which there were still Muslims. That was the case three times, and then there was the case of the Dodecanese in 1947, where there were people who spoke Italian. In all such cases, Greece organised a right of option for Muslims, for Bulgarians as well and also for Italians, so they could express themselves, to decide whether they wanted to have Greek nationality or Turkish, Bulgarian or Italian nationalities. So these are historical cases. But presently, recently I should say, as new events emerge in history, there is a new type of right of option. It is organised by the domestic law of states on an individual basis. In other words, the state puts the question to a specific group of persons, asking whether they want to adopt the nationality of the state, which they can do if they so wish. I quote the example of a recent Slovenian law, which granted such right to all nationals of the former Yugoslavia who were not Slovenes but came from other parts of the former Yugoslavia. Those people lived in or resided in the territory of Slovenia, so such right was granted to Bosnians, to Croats, and there was the possibility of becoming Slovenes. So it was based on internal law. It was the option for one nationality only, for the Slovenian nationality. It is not a pure case of option, but it remains that it is an option that is granted through domestic law. That can be found just about everywhere in the Czech Republic, in Slovakia and also in the former USSR, I believe, which granted the right to specific groups of peoples to opt for a given nationality. There is a very rich practice when it comes to the option of nationality, be it on the basis of an international treaty or on internal law.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think another instance may be the separation of Bangladesh from Pakistan, is that correct Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. That is another example. It can be found also in Surinam, in the world over. But in respect of Bangladesh and Pakistan, there was a right of option organised by Bangladesh, which attributed its nationality to all those deemed by the state to belong to Bangladesh, but Bangladesh said to those who were probably from Pakistan but residing in Bangladesh, said to those that they had the right to opt for the Pakistani nationality within a time period of nine months after the succession, so there is granting of nationality to people who are not nationals of Bangladesh but who live in the territory, who ethnically had common denominators with the state of Pakistan, while those people had the right to opt for the nationality of Pakistan.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Professor, do you have any view on the situation in the former Yugoslavia, where in particular Bosnia-Herzegovina, in terms of the particular groups there, in relation to the right of option in the context of the dissolution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed. In Yugoslavia, each state or each part which became a state after the dissolution of Yugoslavia, settled this matter by way of its internal law. There was no international agreement. I mentioned the case of Slovenia earlier on, which granted the right of option to all residents or non-Slovenian residents living in territory of Slovenia, and the same holds true for Croatia, although I believe there were some stronger conditions. Croatia said that people had to be present in the territory. Those belonging to the Croatian people but who were not Croats had to have a presence in the territory for I believe ten years. I do not know whether this was carried out by the former Republic of Macedonia, I am not that aware of that. As far as Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, I do not think that there was a right of option, as far as I could gather from the examples I read. There was no such right of option. There is law that was passed, I believe, in 1992 and 1993 on nationality, but as far as I can remember there was no right of option granted to specific categories of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: From your understanding of the position in Bosnia-Herzegovina, are any of the conditions arising there -- would any of the conditions that arose there justify the granting of such an option, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, yes, I think that this right of option is justified whenever you have population, or population residing in the territory of the successor state, such population being only religiously -- belonging, religiously or ethnically speaking, to a different community. Whenever there is a different community the right of option must be granted, and in the case in point, there was the Serb community, but you know that the right of option is ruled by two criteria, that is to be found in law. Everywhere the corpus and the animus. The corpus are the objective elements. You have a population which is different from the rest of the population, though it is a population that has a different religion or different ethnic origins or other beliefs. Therefore, this population has features, characteristics that are essentially different from those of the rest of the population, so there we are in the domain of the right of option. But you have to look into the animus of the population. Does the population want to have the right of option or not. As far as I could gather, from what I know as well, I believe that Serbs would have wished to have the right of option to be able to express themselves responsibly for the nationality of Bosnia-Herzegovina or for the nationality of Serbia. So in any case, and that is the rule whenever you can legitimately assume that a group of persons -- not every individual in the group, but parts or major parts of the groups -- do not want to have ex lege the nationality granted by authority, by the successor state, while, respecting the will of the person and of the group, the right of option must be granted. So I say yes to your question that all the conditions were fulfilled for the right of option to exist for the Serb population in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Professor, how important is the perception maintained by one particular group to another group, in one community to another community, in the determination of the issue of nationality on state succession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you know, nationality is a human right. Therefore, it is the person concerned who must have the last word. Nobody else can decide instead of that one person. In situations of state succession you can, for a given period of time, grant or the nationality ex lege, but after that period has elapsed the right of option must be granted. Nationality is something absolutely relevant and major. There is an immediate link between nationality and the person, and each person, each group, will have its own perception of nationality. I know of people in Greece, for instance, who would never envisage changing nationalities, that would be really quite an issue for such people. So basically it is a subjective element, and each person, with their sensitivity, their history, will have their own views of nationality. But we have a guiding principle in this issue; that is that each individual is free to express their views for or against a given nationality; thus, we are talking about an individual right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I want to ask a question of the Professor. You are probably right that everyone should be given the option to exercise whenever there is a case of succession, but until that option is exercised, how would the individual be treated? As a citizen of the new state, or of the parent state? Some time must elapse before the option can be exercised. How would he be treated before that option is exercised, a citizen of the successor state or the parent state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The rule is that the citizen who acquires the nationality after the state succession and attains the nationality of the successor state is a national of the successor state in all sense of the words, without any discrimination. They are on equal footing with the other nationals. There must not be any discrimination between nationals. All must be on the same footing. Of course the question also depends on the assumptions of whether or not the predecessor state continues to exist or whether it has ceased to exist. Such a case -- the right of options, if there are rights of options -- can be played on the level of the successors, and not the predecessor state. In the first case, if the predecessor state does exist the right of option must be offered, either for the predecessor or the successor state. I do not know if I understood absolutely your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I repeat; the right of option on succession -- some time must elapse before the option can be exercised; during the interregnum, an individual living in the succeeding state, would he be treated as a citizen of the succeeding state, or the parent state, during the interregnum before he exercised his option?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This also depends on internal law of the state. According to international practice that I have cited, everybody became a national of the successor state at the very moment of the succession, all at once and automatically. Everybody acquired the nationality of the successor state at the time succession occurred. But a state could then say, "no, you will hold on to your pre -- your successor nationality. Then we will organise right of option so that we can then say that you wanted to have the predecessor state or if you want to acquire the nationality of the successor state". Each state can regulate this and organise it as it wants, that is in relation to the right of option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Professor, do you know what is the legislation in Bosnia on nationality at present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you what I know. I hope that I am not going to make a mistake. I did not read the Bosnian legislation, the laws, not themselves. I have looked through examples in Mr. Mikulka's report in the International Law Commission's work and I can give you the following impressions that I will explain to you. Bosnia-Herzegovina, and first, let us say, in 1992, passed a law and gave its nationality to all those persons who previously had Bosnian citizenship as part of the former Yugoslavia. All Bosnian citizens became nationals of the Bosnian state. But here we see already a gap, because the non-Bosnian residents remained unaccounted for. The non-resident Bosnians, according to the rule that I have just given you, that each of the successor states is obliged to give its nationality to all nationals of the predecessor state that are on its territory, in this case the rule was not applied. But this was remedied a year later by a new law or a decree, I am not sure, at least in some kind of internal Act in 1993, which gave to everybody the right to be a Bosnian national at the very point, so long as that person, or from the point that that person was residing on Bosnian territory. So I think there was a year that evolved between the two, but there was a remedy for it. I do not think there was a right of option in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not in 1992 or in 1993 or even later, at least according to what I know. Let me repeat once more, I did not read the actual Bosnian laws, I did not study this issue and my knowledge comes from reports which I read here and there and might not in fact completely match the facts, which is why I am saying that subject to certain conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. It is possible, Professor, to have different legal concepts of nationality in the international arena. I am wondering about the usage of the word "nationality" in the Geneva Conventions, for instance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, that nationality is a legal concept, that is nationality. But often when, for example, there are two or even three states which claim that they are the national state of the person, or a group of persons; in that case there is another notion which comes into play, which was put forth for the first time by the International Court of Justice in the Notebon case, that is the effectiveness, the idea of effectiveness. There was Liechtenstein, which claimed that Notebon was a national of Liechtenstein. On the other side was Uruguay, saying Notebon was Uruguayan and linked to Uruguay. The court settled the dispute by applying the principle of effective nationality, by stating the issue of what was the country with which he had the closer detachment, what was his real nationality, where did he work, where was his business, where did he have his career. In that case, they tried to find the connections -- not the legal connections, because there were already on both side legal connections, he had both nationalities at the same time -- what was his real, his genuine one. In the end, the court settled the issue by using effectiveness as an example and saying that it was Uruguay because he had many more daily and substantive and real connections with Uruguay than he had with Liechtenstein. Therefore I think, even when there are armed conflicts, the notion of effectiveness that is the belonging, the connection, this is a notion of sovereign law and this is something which can settle ambiguous questions by reviewing things and looking at, seeing at what side the people really were in every day life. I think that this was a guiding principle which is extremely significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any further questions. Any cross-examination so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we mull over it? I think we have asked for the adjournment based on the late notice of his CV. We ask, at a minimum, to start tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There are so many questions which could be asked without even his CV. These are ordinary, simple questions on the nature of the succession itself and the effect of the persons. Unless you are not really keen on any questions? If you are ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Can I confer with my colleagues for a second, within the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me suggest we might take our break now instead of later, so that we can have a conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will come back at 4.30. You will have sufficient consultation. 4.15. (3.40 pm) (Short break) (4.15 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can invite the witness back, please. (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly tell the witness that he is still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still under oath, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours very kindly gave us an opportunity for us to discuss the matter we were discussing before the break amongst ourselves. Although I know each of my friends wants to say something in relation to this matter, the position is this: none of us feels that we are in a proper position properly to cross-examine this witness today. I am going to, if your Honours will indulge me, please, for a moment, just remind you of the history of this matter. Your Honours, the first CV of this gentlemen was supplied to us, as it was indicated by Mr. Turone last week, that was supplied to us on the 1st October. As your Honours will recall, my learned friend Mr. Ackerman told you and it is the case that that CV was two paragraphs long, and by two paragraphs I mean two short paragraphs. It was, in my respectful submission, hopelessly inadequate as a CV of a kind that your Honours were plainly contemplating when you made the order on 27th January, 25th January of this year. I will return to your Honours' order in due course, if I may. The second CV was supplied last week, along with a number of other documents which are pertinent to this matter. That is a document which of course my learned friend Mr. Niemann is right in saying is in one of the official languages of the Tribunal. However, and it may well be that they were not aware of this, in the light of the third CV which has been supplied, that document too can be seen to be hopelessly inadequate. I do not blame them for the second CV in any way at all. That is plainly, it seems to me, the fault of the witness in not providing an adequate CV. However, the first CV that was supplied, as I have indicated, was plainly inadequate, and they most have known that and must have realised it was inadequate. The third CV was supplied this morning, as your Honours know. That document has revealed that it is now probably a proper compliance with your Honours' orders, save as to the question of time. Contained within it, instead of the nine documents, or publications, rather, that the second CV mentioned, this witness has created, mentioned a number of other completely new publications of which we had not heard. I refer to them in particular, which may or may not be of interest to us, depending on what is contained within them. One is said to be an article on the reasons for the conclusion in 1977 of two additional protocols to the international humanitarian law in new international humanitarian law in armed conflicts. That is published in Athens and in Greek. It is a long time since I did any Greek and that was of the ancient variety. Your Honours will see that is a document which is pertinent to this matter and secondly, one we should be entitled to have a look at if we can and secondly to have translated. That will take time. The second document that may interest us, although I do not know at this stage, is the book he wrote in 1956 on the Cyprus question and the right of self determination. Again, your Honours may see that may well be pertinent to the question of will raised by this witness. That was another book not mentioned in the second CV at all. Your Honours, the issue of nationality is an important one. It is plain, in my respectful submission, from the pre-trial brief filed by the Prosecution, from pre-trial briefs filed by Defence counsel, and from the reply that was filed by the Prosecution to those pre-trial briefs, that the issue of nationality is one which you are going to have to deal with in due course. I managed to avoid doing international law at university and in present weeks I have spent some time reading and trying to learn as much as I possibly can about it. It is not a straightforward subject. I expect my detractors would say, "that is because you are not very bright and you do not understand it". The reality is it is not a straightforward subject and one which takes a little time to grasp. This comes to the nub of it. It is an important matter. This witness has, probably through his own fault, failed to provide an adequate CV in the terms of your Honours' order. I remind you of the order. It is to timely notice of the expert witnesses, the name of the witness, the witness' CV and a statement of the areas about which the witness will testify. I return to that last phrase, because looking at the application made by my learned friend Mr. Turone, he tells us what the subject was going to be in a total of four words "state succession and nationality". That is about as uninformative as it possibly could be. So it is not until today that we have any idea at all first of all what the text of the evidence is going to be and what the import of it is going to be. Your Honour, none of us feel that we are in a properly prepared position or that we have had adequate time to prepare to cross-examine this witness. I rely in particular, but not exclusively, upon those two articles that I have mentioned to you as being those about which we have only found about today, both of which are both plainly pertinent to this subject. Your Honour, if this means the witness has to come back next week and it is inconvenient to him, then he only has himself to blame for failing to provide a proper CV to the Prosecution. If he cavils at the suggestion he has to come back this week, your Honours, of course, as has been made plain in the court, have powers to make him come back next week if so required. In our respectful submission, this is an issue which goes fundamentally to the question of whether or not the defendant is going to be given a fair trial on a matter of considerable importance. We respectfully submit that it would on this occasion be a proper way in which to deal with this matter to grant an adjournment so that the Defence can have an adequate time properly to prepare to cross-examine this witness. We have in mind that this case should be adjourned until Wednesday of next week to enable us to secure these documents and have them translated from Greek. Your Honour, that is our application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you really suggesting that from the expert evidence we have here so far you have been so startled that you can do nothing to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It is not a question of doing nothing, it is doing it properly and in one go. One would hate to discover next week that the articles this gentlemen has written contain a number of either completely contrary statements compared with his evidence, or that there was something extremely helpful in them and that we have been deprived of the opportunity to put those in proper context.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Counsel and Mr. Landzo support our colleague Michael Greaves in his submission that we believe we could be ready by next Wednesday. I would like to add also that it is unfortunate that it would be inconvenient for Professor Economides to have to return next week, but so that due process might be seen, as was evident with General Pasalic, who was here under subpoena at violation of his religious beliefs, that sometimes those things become necessary when there is a scheme this large going on that affects so many different people. We ask also that so that due process can be had for our accused I am sure you know that if one of these documents shows up that he said something contrary. It is not important that we do not understand what he is saying today but it might be important for impeachment purposes if he has contradicted himself. We ask this court to please allow us a few days to prepare. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, joining with my friends, I might add one thing, that the short synopsis of what we were given that he was going to talk about was trying to guess what he was going to say was similar to reading tea leaves. In thinking about his testimony, I related it to a response to a pre-trial memo that Mr. Dixon filed back in April and thought that it might be prepared back in April that his testimony would be along those lines, which is something different from what he has testified to, a different subject area, completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, on behalf of Mr. Delalic, we would adopt the submissions by our learned friend Mr. Greaves on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are saying that you are unable to cross-examine today, until some time next week. That is all you are saying. Yes, let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, firstly it is regrettable that it is necessary to attack the witness for the alleged shortcomings in the CV. The CV that was supplied -- as I said earlier, the name was given. If anything else was required it was incumbent upon counsel, if they needed this information, to at least go to the extent of trying to make telephone contact. As I understand it, the witness says he is not available next week. What that entails I do not know your Honours, but it seems to me that the examination-in-chief was relatively short. It covered an area which I would have thought counsel would have had to have been appraised of for the purposes of defending this case in any event, such were the issues of importance. I would not have thought that cross-examination was impossible in these circumstances. It seems to me that if the research was carried out by counsel and something was subsequently discovered which would necessitate further cross-examination at some later date then the appropriate course would be for them to proceed with their cross-examination now and if they discover other matters which would necessitate this witness being brought back, then those matters could be raised at the appropriate time. This witness need not be discharged at the end of cross-examination. The witness could be informed that should matters arise which would require him to be recalled then that can happen and those matters can be put to him. I just think, your Honours, that it is impossible to -- not impossible, I am not saying it is not impossible to proceed with cross-examination now. They can do so. The concerns they have can be remedied by this course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When next are you sure you might be able to get the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the course of the break I had someone speak to the witness because he was -- I did not speak to him myself, but I was told he could come back if necessary in the first week of December when there is a week set aside for this case, if it was to go that long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose in the interest of justice, and at least to enable counsel to prepare, we might adjourn the witness' cross-examination until that time; except you want to start now and conclude at that time. But if you do not want to then it might be then. I hope we do not have the same problems with Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If we are to have the same problems with Dr. Gow, your Honour, I think it be appropriate they be raised and discussed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to appraise the Trial Chamber, we have talked somewhat about some publications in Jayne's publications by Mr. Gow. Over the lunch-break I finally managed to get into my e-mail and determine that Jayne's is being slow about sending them to me, for reasons known only to Jayne's publications. We have not received them yet. I do not know when we will receive them. I believe it is nine separate publications by Mr. Gow that are relevant to the competence of the Tribunal. I do not know how long they are. I can tell you that they are œ15 each, is basically what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour knows I have raised this matter on two prior occasions. Let me tell you the current status. On the day that this Tribunal granted the Prosecutor's request to call Mr. Gow we immediately transmitted a list, his CV with his list of publications, to a representative of the librarian of this Tribunal and asked that those articles be acquired and made available to us. That process is going on. I have received -- without having it in front of me I cannot give you numbers -- I have received maybe five of fifteen. None of the Jayne's publications that Tom talks about have been received and those may be the most relevant. The last word that we had from the library of this court was that we could expect the balance of the documents next week. Whether or not they will arrive in a manner that is sufficiently in advance of the need to cross-examine Dr. Gow to allow us to get them through them all or not is right now an open question. I wish I could say that we had all the documents and we have three or four days and we will be ready. I cannot say that. I cannot say that I will not be raising this issue next week if I have not got all those documents. I know that the librarian of this court is working diligently to try to get them to me and that has been going on for some time and is ongoing. That is the best I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as Professor Gow is concerned, the position is somewhat better than in the case of Professor Economides, because Dr. Gow has already appeared before this Tribunal and we have access to his literature, and I am referring to the past two or three months during which time I have been studying the problem. But to ask us at this point whether we will be entirely ready ... I must say that I cannot answer that question. We have to be cautious, but in the interest of justice and economy and, of course, the possibilities of Dr. Gow to come before the Tribunal again, we will be ready to cross-examine him. As far as the indulgence of the court is concerned, and your agreement to call the Professor back in December, we should like to express our appreciation to your Honours for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I asked the question because I felt both the Prosecution and the Defence both together have a duty towards the Trial Chamber to make sure that things work properly and efficiently in the interest of justice. That is why, instead of one trying to take advantage of it. That is why I ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I totally and completely agree with what you just said. Many of these problems, with the efforts of the librarian to get these documents, would be easily solved if the Prosecution have them and would copy them and give them to us. I think they may well have them. The man has testified here on at least three prior occasions; on all those three occasions he has been led by Mr. Niemann. I would be very surprised if Mr. Niemann does not have in his possession all of those writings. All this could be solved if they could copy them and give them to us, rather than going through this round about, time-consuming procedure of getting them. If they do not have them -- I agree with you, co-operation would solve a lot of these problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose since nothing is happening we terminate this witness' questioning till a more convenient date when perhaps you are sure both of these things will be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the sake of trying to resolve this, do we understand that we will be responsible for finding Dr. Gow's publications, or is the Prosecution in a position to provide them with us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Tribunal is not involved in the financial aspect of your case. You know how to do it. We do not discuss that. You know who to go to for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The basis upon which it is alleged I have them is predicated on a false premise. I will be telling them that in a letter that I am writing to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, what do we have tomorrow, let us assess that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours seeing as we adjourn at 5.30, I could try to make efforts to get the custodian of records here now. It may be -- he has got to get from his hotel to here. We could go on this afternoon with the custodian of records. It may take about 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: To get him here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am told the Victims and Witnesses Unit apparently need half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It will not be necessary to make that effort. We can start with him tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, are we to call Dr. Gow next week? If I can make some inquiries and see if I can get this material which yes, I did have at one stage and I looked for at lunch time and do not have at the moment. If we get it and do give it to the Defence tomorrow, is it going to be sufficient? Because Dr. Gow is due to fly in on Saturday morning, his ticket is booked and everything arranged. If the Defence are going to stand up on Monday or Tuesday after the evidence-in-chief and say they are not ready to cross-examine, then I suggest that Dr. Gow go over to the 1st December as well. They must know how long it is going to take them to read this material. They know the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that will not be quite right. If he is coming at all let him come also and give his evidence and might still postpone the cross-examination until December.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that makes it very difficult for us to -- the normal course is for cross-examination to follow immediately after evidence-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, that is where it is facilitating even the evidence itself; when in fact it makes it more complex I do not think it is wise to do that now, if he comes in and his cross-examination continues, or the parties are unable to cross-examine at all, as we have now seen in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My understanding is they have said they are not ready to cross-examine. That being the case, if they are simply not ready now, are they going to be ready over the weekend? If they are not going to be ready ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to answer Mr. Niemann's question. If in fact Mr. Niemann has the materials and gets them to me tomorrow I think there is enough time between now and perhaps next Tuesday for me to digest the balance of those materials. I have already spent a significant amount of time working on this matter. It is the absence of somewhat, I consider, important materials that is the issue right now. If they are available to me tomorrow then I suspect that I can be prepared by Tuesday of next week to do a cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So this is an assurance that the Gow situation might not be the same as in this present case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may not be the same because it is question of when the materials are available. I am only speaking for myself, I am not speaking for any other counsel here. For my own purposes, if Mr. Niemann can make those materials available to me tomorrow, I think I will have time to digest them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As it applies at least to Jayne's materials, I again, over the lunch hour, sent an e-mail back to Jayne's, saying, "please send them, please fax them immediately, do it". It is possible, it is possible we can go back in the Defence room and they will be coming off the fax machine now, it is possible they will be here at 10 o'clock tomorrow morning. We are doing everything we can independently to obtain access to those materials, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We take it that Gow's evidence will go on as indicated, until something changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May I make a suggestion as well, please? In relation to this witness Professor Economides, it may well be that he is the person who is best in the position to provide us a copy of the 1989 article that was published in Greek which concerns the two additional protocols to the Geneva Conventions. He may be able to assist us all by providing us with a copy quicker than almost in any way in which we could obtain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps all you need is the publications and you might be able to trace how to get it. He does not keep copies of his articles. I do not know that so many people do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I suspect, your Honour, that most academics do, your Honour, but that is by the by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in connection with Professor Gow, we are in the same position as my colleagues; but if we are talking about the timetable for next week, could the Prosecution please tell us whether, in addition to Dr. Gow, there will be other witnesses and who they are, because we do not have that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann, are you able to assist here, so that they will know what to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. Your Honours, there is some uncertainty as to, at this stage, whether or not there be additional witnesses to Professor Gow, or Dr. Gow, and I will hopefully be in a position tomorrow morning to announce those witnesses. It pertains to a matter related to the proceedings but not directly connected to eyewitness testimony as such. But I will be in a position tomorrow morning to provide that information. I just wish to emphasise that the material that we have on Dr. Gow may not include -- may or may not include -- all the Jayne's material that Mr. Moran looks for. So I really do have to emphasise that whatever -- if we are able to put material together to give to them, it may not be what they want. I need to say that now, because I am not confident that we have everything that they think that we do have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They might have indicated what they are looking for, have they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They have indicated they want publications from Jayne's Military Journal. I am not sure we have all that. A lot of it, I am not sure it is relevant. It is material I may have read in London when I did my initial research into Dr. Gow and his publications. I did a lot of it in London and did not bring it back here. I am not sure I had a lot of here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If the Prosecution is not a position -- we cannot expect them to create it. They would have the same problem getting it as we would, under the rule of reasonableness. One thing I would ask, the first question I intend to ask Professor Economides on cross-examination is if he sent any reports or synopsis of what he believes international law is to the Office of the Prosecutor related to his testimony. If he were to say yes to that, I would immediately ask for a copy of it. So, if such a thing exists it might be appropriate that some time this week next week to have it delivered. I am not saying it exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You started from a position in which you are so handicapped that you can say nothing. It is difficult for one to say anything now. If we started anywhere and you found out you were unable to go forward at some stage then I would have now understood this position that you are now taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What I am saying is if it turns out in the first week of December Professor Economides says yes, I wrote a 15-page report to the Prosecutor's Office about nationality and the former Yugoslavia, at that point someone might be asking for another adjournment while they read that. I am not saying it exists, because I have no idea one way or another, but if such a thing like that exists it might be appropriate to consider the statement under Rule 66A and have it produced in the next few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I can confirm that there is no such report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise and will assemble at 10 o'clock tomorrow. (4.55 pm) (Adjourned until 10.00 am on Friday 31st October 1997) 23 24 25
